description: We're a team from Loudoun County, Virginia who like turning real NASA data into tools people can actually use, with skills in web development, data analysis and finance.
summary:
Don't predict the next season with a groundhog. Replay the last 45.

Farmers choose a specific crop rotation years ahead, and a forecast cannot be checked. Replay45 takes every rotation that farmers near a field, or farmers in the place that used to have its weather, could grow, and runs each one through 45 real seasons of NASA weather (1981-2025) for each area. It then measures each rotation the way an investor measures a portfolio: average result, bad-year result, and which crops fail in the same years, in crop and in dollars.

Nothing is forecast and nothing is a black box. Every option shows the pros and cons, what the tool does not know, and what to ask a local agronomist. REPLAY-45 assists farmers to let their field see another season.
details:
THE PROBLEM

A crop rotation is a multi-year commitment made on experience from past seasons. This is becoming increasingly difficult in a climate that is changing. Most tools answer with a forecast or an AI recommendation, which a farmer cannot verify. A farmer can better believe predictions based on past history.

WHAT IT DOES

1. Field brief. Four plain sentences: what the current rotation brings in during a bad year, the hardest seasons on record, which crop holds up when the main crop fails, and how many tested rotations do better.

2. All rotations compared. Every rotation of one to four years built from the crop menu, with and without a rye cover crop, is replayed on the field's soil through NASA POWER daily weather for 1981-2025. Each is one dot on a chart: crop in a one-in-ten bad year against water shortfall. For our two fields that is 361 and 741 rotations, about 180,000 field-seasons.

3. Worst seasons. The three hardest seasons in the field's own record, with what each rotation would have harvested.

4. Risk and return. Average result, volatility, return per unit of risk, bad-year result, worst year and longest slump, a table of which crops fail in the same years, and gross revenue per acre from prices the farmer can edit.

5. Where the crop menu comes from. Crops grown near the field, plus crops grown where the field's 2006-2025 climate was normal in 1981-2000 (a climate match from NASA POWER). Both come from the USDA Cropland Data Layer.

6. Check against satellite data. The replay is compared with summer greenness measured by NASA MODIS at the field.

7. Farmer controls. Priority sliders for water, steady yields and soil; rain-only or irrigated; a yearly water limit; a "same seasons with less rain" what-if; crops switched off when there is no buyer or equipment; build-your-own rotation; editable prices; US or metric units.

HOW IT WORKS

A 10-day soil water balance: FAO-56 Penman-Monteith evapotranspiration, FAO-56 crop coefficients, SCS curve-number runoff and FAO-33 yield response to water, with frost, heat and ripening checks, on the field's USDA SSURGO soil. Each rotation is run once per starting year of its cycle and the runs are pooled.

WHAT WE FOUND

Cozad, Nebraska sits on the 100th meridian, the old line between the rainy East and the dry West. On rain alone, the local corn-corn-soybean rotation brings in about 40% of a full crop in a one-in-ten bad year. 104 of the 361 rotations tested do better on both bad-year crop and water shortfall.

Corn and soybeans fail in the same years. Their yearly harvests have a correlation of 0.92 on this field, so rotating them cuts year-to-year swings by only about 1%. Winter wheat holds up best when corn fails (0.47), because it grows in a different season.

The replay found the droughts by itself. Given weather numbers only, it ranks 2002, 2012 and 2022 as Cozad's hardest seasons, all known Nebraska drought years.

The steadier rotation earns less. At Cozad, corn-corn-soybean grosses about $493 an acre in an average year and $298 in a bad year. The rotation borrowed from the climate match (corn-fallow-winter wheat) is steadier but grosses about $262 and $170. The tool shows both sides of that trade.

Loudoun County, Virginia is our home county. Water is rarely short there, so the question is how many crops a field can grow in a year. Its closest farmed climate match is across the Potomac in Maryland, where farmers grow corn, then winter wheat followed by double-crop soybean. In Loudoun's driest season on record (2007), that borrowed rotation would have harvested about 1.0 full crop against 0.74 for the local soybean-corn rotation, and it grosses more: about $701 an acre on average against $664.

We tested a famous claim. A 2018 study estimated the arid-humid boundary has moved about 140 miles east of the 100th meridian. Tracing the same moisture index in NASA data for 1981-2000 against 2006-2025, we find an average of only 4 miles east. We report it as it is.

A what-if. Replaying Cozad's same 45 seasons with 20% less rain drops the local rotation's bad-year crop from 40% to 30%.

HOW IT ANSWERS THE CHALLENGE

- NASA Earth observations: NASA POWER weather drives every replay; NASA MODIS greenness shows bare-ground windows and checks the replay.

- Local soil: USDA SSURGO water-holding capacity and runoff group for each field.

- Crop characteristics: planting window, rooting depth, water sensitivity, frost and heat limits for 10 crops.

- Farmer priorities and constraints: sliders, water supply and limit, crop switches, editable prices, build-your-own rotation.

- At least three rotations including the existing one: hundreds replayed, four shown in detail, the current one first.

- Why, evidence, benefits, gaps and risks: on every detailed card, with questions for an extension agent.

- Soil health: days with no living cover, heavy rains on bare ground, legumes, crop variety, a cover-crop version of every rotation.

- Changing conditions: 1981-2000 against 2006-2025 throughout, the climate match, the worst seasons, the less-rain what-if.

- Plain language: a glossary and a table of what satellites can and cannot see of one field.

- Supports, does not replace, judgment: no rotation is named the answer.

LIMITS, STATED IN THE TOOL

Dollar figures are gross revenue from US-average prices and yields, before costs, so they are not profit. No pests or nutrients are modelled. Yields are relative potential from typical crop values, not local varieties. One soil and one 250 m satellite pixel per field. The satellite agreement is moderate (r = 0.40 at Cozad, 0.49 at Loudoun). No farmer has tested the tool yet. Measuring rotations as portfolios is established in research; our contribution is an open, single-file version for US fields driven by NASA weather.

BUILT WITH

One self-contained HTML file (JavaScript, SVG, canvas, d3-geo) and a Python script that downloads the data. The code was written with the help of an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic).

AI Usage Disclosure

Our team utilized artificial intelligence tools throughout the development of REPLAY-45 to accelerate development, support problem-solving, and improve the overall quality of our solution. AI served as an assistive tool, not a replacement for our team's original ideas, research, and planning.

1. User Experience

Claude: This was used to assist with website UI/UX.

2. Content and Documentation

Claude additionally assisted with the code in index.html and fetch_data.py

3. Human Oversight and Original Contributions. 

All AI-assisted outputs were evaluated by our team before being incorporated into the final project. We retained responsibility for the project's technical decisions, scientific reasoning, implementation, and validation.

The fundamental concept, project direction, core functionality, and final solution were developed and directed by our team. AI tools served as supplementary resources to improve development efficiency and support our work, not to replace the engineering and problem-solving contributions of our team.
